title: My father gave me cash and two houses. Should I buy my next property in cash or with a loan?
shortTitle: Cash or loan with family money
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #228 | INHERITANCE OF ASSETS WORTH MILLIONS
excerpt: A 23-year-old earning RM3,500 has been given cash, shares and two houses, and wants a RM200,000 to RM300,000 apartment. The parents say pay cash; Sean says use the two 90% loans and keep the cash.

qa.asker: M, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: M is 23 and earns RM3,500 a month. M's father has given M RM800,000 in cash, RM500,000 in shares, RM130,000 in a unit trust and two houses worth about RM1.2 million; the family owns five other properties, mostly bought in cash. M wants to buy an apartment in Cheras for about RM200,000 to RM300,000 as an investment, with an instalment of about RM1,300, but M's parents would rather pay cash to save interest.
qa.question: Is it better to buy with a loan or in cash, and can M take housing loans for two properties at once on this salary?
qa.quote: Your active income will be the limiting factor.
qa.answer: Use loans for the first two purchases, while the 90% margin is available, and leave the cash in fixed deposits; the tenant's rent pays the interest. Buy one at a time: after about six months of rent records the bank counts the rent as income for the next loan. Cash comes in later, for a third property at 70% and for furnishing.

reasons.title: Cheap loans favour leverage
reasons.body: M's parents bought when interest rates were around 10% to 12%, so paying cash made sense. With rates far lower, it's better to use the bank's money and keep the cash working.

reasons.title: Rent becomes income
reasons.body: If the rent is a little above the instalment, the surplus adds to M's income for the next loan once there is a tenancy agreement and six months of payments. Two loans at once won't pass on RM3,500 a month.

reasons.title: Cash has its turn later
reasons.body: The third housing loan is capped at 70%, so a RM500,000 unit needs about RM150,000 down; furnishing a RM300,000 subsale to let may cost RM30,000 to RM40,000. The gifted houses can also be refinanced, if M's income supports it.

reasons.title: Income is the real limit
reasons.body: Every loan and refinance depends on M's own income, so building skills and a career matters as much as the assets. Having more to lose also means more care: learn, take advice and run due diligence.

actions: Buy the first unit with a loan, but only if the rent covers the instalment.
Keep the cash in fixed deposits and leave the shares as they are while you learn.
Set a furnishing budget for each unit so it rents well from day one.
Wait about six months after letting the first unit before applying for the second loan.
Learn how rental and dividend income are declared and taxed, so they count towards future loans.
qa.caveat: Sean respects the parents' cash approach, which suited the high rates of their time. The plan depends on the rent covering each instalment; if it doesn't, paying more upfront is the safer route.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #228. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in October 2023. The captions don't make clear whether the asker is a man or a woman, so the article uses 'M' throughout.
